lead: A velocity field gives a speed and a direction at every point of a flow. Three kinds of curve draw that field on paper: the streamline, tangent to the velocity at one instant; the pathline, the track of one particle over time; and the streakline, the line of dye released from one point. Engineers use them to sketch flow through pipes and around bodies, and to read flow-visualisation photographs. The three are the same curve only when the flow is steady.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the Eulerian velocity components u, v, w, and Chapter 2.2 for what steady flow means.

sections.h3: Three drawings of one velocity field

blocks.text: In the Eulerian view a flow is a field: at every fixed point and every instant there is a velocity vector with components u, v and w, in m/s, along the axes x, y and z, in metres. The same field can be drawn in three ways. A general name for all three drawings is flow lines.

items: Streamline: a curve that, at one chosen instant, is tangent to the velocity at every point on it.
Pathline: the actual track traced by one marked fluid particle over a period of time.
Streakline: at one instant, the line joining all the particles that have already passed through one chosen fixed point.

blocks.text: What each drawing holds fixed makes the difference. A streamline freezes time and shows the whole field at that instant. A pathline freezes one particle and shows its history. A streakline freezes the release point and shows where all its visitors have reached. Dye from a nozzle in a water channel gives a streakline. A long-exposure photograph of a single tracer gives a pathline.

sections.h3: The streamline never crosses (except at a stagnation point)

blocks.text: Take a point where the velocity is V = ui + vj + wk. A small element of the streamline through that point is dr = dxi + dyj + dzk. For the curve to be tangent to the velocity, dr must be parallel to V, so dr × V = 0. Written out, this gives the streamline equation.

blocks.where: u, v, w are the velocity components in m/s along x, y, z in metres; dx, dy, dz are the increments of the curve in metres. In two dimensions it becomes dy/dx = v/u, the slope of the streamline in the xy-plane.

blocks.text: Solving this first-order differential equation gives a family of curves with one constant. The point through which the streamline must pass fixes that constant, exactly as in the worked example below.

Two streamlines cannot cross. If they did, the crossing point would have two tangents, so the fluid there would need two velocities at once. The one exception is a stagnation point, where u = v = w = 0, the direction is undefined, and streamlines may meet and split.

A bundle of neighbouring streamlines forms a stream tube. Fluid cannot cross the tube wall, because the wall runs along the velocity everywhere. The tube behaves like a pipe with no leakage, and the discharge through every section of it is the same (see Chapter 2.5).

sections.h3: Pathline, streakline, and when all three merge

blocks.text: A pathline follows one particle. If the particle is at (x, y, z) at time t, its path obeys the three equations below, integrated with time.
dx/dt = u,  dy/dt = v,  dz/dt = w
blocks.where: u, v, w are the velocity components in m/s at the particle's position and at that same time t; x, y, z are the particle's coordinates in metres and t is in seconds.

blocks.text: A streakline is the photograph of a dye filament. Fix the release point P. Every particle that has passed through P leaves a visible dot; the curve through all those dots at one instant is the streakline. Smoke rising from an incense stick in still room air is a streakline: it marks the trail of particles that left the tip, not the future path of any one of them.

In steady flow the velocity at a fixed point does not change with time. A particle released at P then follows a fixed curve, every later particle released at P follows the same curve, and the instant photograph of arrivals is that curve too. So streamline, pathline and streakline all coincide. In unsteady flow they generally differ.
Exam habit: name the flow first. Steady flow, and you may use any of the three names for the one curve. Unsteady flow, and the question is asking which of the three it wants.

figure.caption: One velocity field drawn three ways: the streamline shows the instant, the pathline one particle, the streakline one release point. They merge into a single curve only in steady flow.

spec.aria: The three flow lines differ by whether they show an instant, one particle, or a history of arrivals.

examples.question: A steady two-dimensional velocity field has u = 2x m/s and v = 3y m/s, where x and y are in metres. Find the equation of the streamline passing through the point (1 m, 2 m). Hence find the value of y on this streamline at x = 2 m and at x = 4 m.
steps: Check steadiness: u and v contain no t, so the field is steady and the streamline is a fixed curve in space.
Slope of the streamline: dy/dx = v/u = 3y/(2x).
Integrate both sides: ln y = 1.5 ln x + ln C, so y = C x^1.5, with C in m^(−0.5).
Apply the point (1, 2): 2 = C(1)^1.5, so C = 2 m^(−0.5).
Streamline through (1, 2): y = 2x^1.5, with x and y in metres.
examples.answer: The streamline is y = 2x^1.5 with x and y in metres; it passes through y = 5.657 m at x = 2 m and y = 16 m at x = 4 m.

examples.question: A dye filament is photographed in a flow where the velocity at a fixed point changes with time. The photograph shows a straight line, but streamlines drawn for the same region at that instant are curved. Is this possible, and why?
steps: The photograph of a dye filament records a streakline: it joins all particles that earlier left the injection point.
Each particle left the point at a different time and travelled through a region where the velocity was changing.
So the streakline is a record of past velocities, not of the velocity field at the present instant.
The streamline is drawn from the velocity field at the present instant only.
In unsteady flow the two are different curves, so a straight streakline with curved streamlines is possible.
Only in steady flow would both have to be the same curve.
examples.answer: Yes. In unsteady flow the streakline records past velocities while the streamline records the present field, so the two curves need not match.

traps: Drawing two streamlines that cross. They can meet only at a stagnation point, where the velocity is zero and the direction is undefined.
Assuming the pathline and the streamline are the same curve in unsteady flow. They coincide only in steady flow; in unsteady flow, state which curve you mean.
Quoting the family y = C x^1.5 and stopping there. The given point must be substituted to fix C, or the answer is incomplete.
Turning the slope upside down. In the xy-plane the streamline slope is dy/dx = v/u, not u/v.
Calling a steady dye filament a pathline. At any instant a dye filament is a streakline; it equals a pathline only because the flow is steady.

quiz.a: A curve that is tangent to the instantaneous velocity direction at every point on it, at one chosen instant of time.

quiz.q: Define a streakline in one sentence.
quiz.a: At one instant, the locus of all particles that have earlier passed through a given fixed point in the flow.

quiz.q: Why can two streamlines not cross, and where is the exception?
quiz.a: At a crossing point the curve would need two tangents, so the fluid would need two velocities at one point, which is impossible. The exception is a stagnation point, where u = v = w = 0, so the direction is undefined and streamlines may meet.

quiz.q: In steady flow, why do the streamline, pathline and streakline coincide?
quiz.a: In steady flow the velocity at each fixed point does not change with time. A particle released at a point P therefore follows a fixed curve, every later particle released at P follows the same curve, and the instantaneous picture of all arrivals from P is that same curve.

quiz.q: A steady field has u = 2x m/s and v = 3y m/s. Find the streamline through the point (2 m, 3 m).
quiz.a: dy/dx = v/u = 3y/(2x), giving y = C x^1.5. Substituting (2, 3): 3 = C(2)^1.5 = 2.828 C, so C = 1.061 m^(−0.5). Streamline: y = 1.061 x^1.5, x and y in metres.

quiz.q: For the field u = 2x m/s, v = 3y m/s, find the slope dy/dx of the streamline at the point (1 m, 2 m).
quiz.a: dy/dx = v/u = 3(2)/(2(1)) = 6/2 = 3. The streamline rises 3 m in y for every 1 m in x at that point.

quiz.q: Smoke from an incense stick in a room rises as a thin wavy line. Which flow line does it show, and would a photograph of it equal the streamlines of the room air?
quiz.a: It is a streakline: it marks every particle that has left the tip. The room air has draughts and temperature changes, so the flow is unsteady; the streakline then records past velocities and generally differs from the instantaneous streamlines. Only if the air were perfectly steady would all three curves be the same.

beyond: Not for the exam. Streakline visualisation with dye and smoke is still used in wind-tunnel testing, and particle image velocimetry replaces the long-exposure pathline with two short laser flashes, giving the instantaneous velocity field. The same three curves appear in environmental work on pollutant plumes, where the streakline from a chimney is what a monitoring station actually samples. Search for particle image velocimetry, flow visualisation dye streakline, and streamline vs pathline in unsteady flow.
